lesson.title: Does the Data Fit the Model? The Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test
lesson.summary: The chi-square goodness-of-fit test uses the chi-square statistic to test whether a single categorical variable follows a claimed distribution of proportions, following the same hypothesize, check conditions, calculate, conclude structure as any hypothesis test.
lesson.body:
A goodness-of-fit test, often abbreviated GOF, is one specific and common use of the chi-square statistic: it tests whether a single categorical variable follows some hypothesized distribution across its categories. It follows the same general four-step structure as any hypothesis test (state hypotheses, check conditions, calculate a test statistic and p-value, state a conclusion in context), now filled in with chi-square specific details.

Two conditions need to hold before the test result can be trusted. First, the counts should come from a random sample or a genuinely random process, and observations need to be independent of one another. Second, every expected count should be at least 5, sometimes called the large counts condition, because the chi-square distribution is only a good approximation to the true, discrete sampling distribution of the statistic when expected counts are not too small. When both conditions hold, the chi-square statistic computed from the data follows approximately a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of categories minus 1.

Finishing the die example from chi-square statistic: H0 is that the die is fair, meaning each face has true probability 1 divided by 6. Ha is that the die is not fair, meaning at least one face's true probability differs from 1 divided by 6. All six expected counts equal 10, comfortably above 5, so the large counts condition is met, and rolls of a physical die can reasonably be treated as independent trials. The chi-square statistic, computed earlier, is 3.8. Degrees of freedom is the number of categories minus 1, or 6 minus 1 equals 5. The critical value for a significance level of 0.05 at df equals 5 is 11.070. Since 3.8 is far below 11.070, the result is nowhere near significant. Technology gives a p-value of roughly 0.58 for this statistic and these degrees of freedom, a large p-value by any standard. Because that p-value is so much bigger than any reasonable significance level, we fail to reject H0. This data is entirely consistent with a fair die, the deviations observed, like 14 fours instead of 10, are well within the range of ordinary random variation.

One directional detail is worth flagging explicitly: the goodness-of-fit test always rejects for large chi-square values, meaning large mismatches between observed and expected, and it never rejects for a suspiciously small chi-square statistic. Data that fits the null hypothesis unusually well is not, by itself, evidence against that hypothesis in this framework, even though in rare situations an extremely small chi-square value might raise separate concerns, such as whether the data were fabricated, that fall outside the standard test logic.
